title: Given a set of numbers that may contain duplicates, generate all possible unique subsets, with no two subsets identical. Explain how sorting plus a controlled expansion of only the newly added subsets prevents duplicate subsets.
shortTitle: Subsets With Duplicates (Generate Unique Subsets When Elements Repeat)
keyPoints: Sort the input first so equal elements are adjacent, which is a hard precondition for the duplicate-skip rule.
For a non-duplicate element, extend all existing subsets; for a duplicate, extend only the subsets added in the previous round.
Tracking the previous round start index controls which subsets receive the duplicate element.
The technique produces each distinct subset exactly once in O(n * 2^n) time.
Without sorting, the adjacency assumption breaks and duplicates cannot be reliably skipped.
The same approach works in both iterative doubling and backtracking with a skip condition.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort first, and for a repeated element extend only the subsets added in the previous round to avoid duplicate subsets.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Subsets With Duplicates** – generates every distinct subset when the input may contain repeated elements.
- **Sort precondition** – sorting places equal values next to each other, enabling the duplicate-skip rule.
- **Iterative doubling** – for each element, copy and extend existing subsets; for a duplicate, restrict this to subsets created in the previous round.
- **Previous-round tracking** – store the start index of the previous round so only those subsets get the new duplicate appended.
- **Complexity** – proportional to the number of distinct subsets produced, which is at most 2^n.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has available cashback coupons that may include duplicates, like two identical five-percent coupons. When marketing enumerates every distinct coupon bundle, choosing the first five-percent coupon or the second must not count as two different bundles. Rajesh sorts the coupons so identical ones sit together, and when he processes a repeat he only grows the bundles that already received the previous identical coupon.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Input: [1, 2, 2]  (sorted)

Round 0 (start):   result = [ [] ]

Round 1 (element 1, new):
  Extend ALL subsets:  [] + 1 = [1]
  result = [ [], [1] ]
  previousRoundStart = 0

Round 2 (element 2, new):
  Extend ALL subsets:  [] + 2 = [2],  [1] + 2 = [1,2]
  result = [ [], [1], [2], [1,2] ]
  previousRoundStart = 2

Round 3 (element 2, DUPLICATE):
  Extend ONLY from index 2:  [2] + 2 = [2,2],  [1,2] + 2 = [1,2,2]
  result = [ [], [1], [2], [1,2], [2,2], [1,2,2] ]

Final: 6 distinct subsets, no duplicates
```

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        Duplicate-Skip Decision Flow             │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                │
│   For each element nums[i]:                    │
│       │                                        │
│       ▼                                        │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐             │
│   │ nums[i] == nums[i-1] ?      │             │
│   └──────────────────────────────┘             │
│       │ Yes              │ No                  │
│       ▼                  ▼                     │
│   start = prevStart   start = 0               │
│   (only new subsets)  (all subsets)            │
│       │                  │                     │
│       └──────┬───────────┘                     │
│              ▼                                 │
│   Extend subsets[start..size-1]                │
│   Update previousRoundStart = size             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets With Duplicates generates every distinct subset when the input may contain repeated elements, and the challenge is to avoid producing the same subset twice. The solution has a hard precondition: sort the input so that equal elements sit next to each other. Without sorting, the adjacency assumption breaks and the algorithm cannot detect duplicates.

The iterative approach starts with a result list containing only the empty subset. For each element, it copies eligible subsets, appends the current element, and adds the new subsets to the result. When the current element is new, all existing subsets are eligible. When it equals the previous element, only the subsets created in the previous round are eligible. This restriction is what prevents duplicates: a second copy of a value must attach only to subsets that already contain the first copy.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to enumerate distinct cashback-coupon bundles for customers whose baskets could contain identical coupons. Marketing needed each real bundle listed once rather than duplicated by which identical coupon was chosen. Sorting the coupons, extending only the previous round on repeats, and producing clean distinct bundles solved the problem.

The backtracking approach achieves the same result with a recursive skip condition: within the same recursion level, skip an element if it equals the previous one. Both approaches require sorting and produce the same output.

Remember one sentence: sort the array, and for a duplicate element, extend only the subsets from the previous round rather than all existing subsets.
